extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly (scientists, educated general public, students)
extracted.subtask_description: Writing and compiling short book notices, scientific reports, and popular-science miscellany items for a general-educated-magazine audience; includes guidance on what makes useful manuals, reports, and short scientific notes. Emphasizes methods of presentation, evidence, and practical implications for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: State purpose and scope briefly but satisfactorily
rubrics_metrics.description: The book aims to tell, as briefly as is possible consistently with giving a satisfactory statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present points briefly and clearly; arrange material by departments/chapters covering particular aspects; enforce points by reference to particular law or decision (for legal subjects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange material by clear chapters/departments
rubrics_metrics.description: The author has examined more than a thousand legal authorities ... and has arranged the whole mass of information ... in chapters, each of which covers a particular department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize a large mass of information into coherent, departmentally-organized chapters so each covers a particular subject-area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relate local focus to general principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The work has been prepared with especial reference to the city and the State of New York, but the principles it embodies are of general application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a work is prepared with a particular jurisdictional reference, show how underlying principles generalize beyond the local focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical analysis: emphasize causation and continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: "The principle is kept in view throughout that the bearing and meaning of every event are largely determined by the events that preceded it... By knowing this relation, the inquirer learns not merely what took place, but why it took place."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat personalities as results of prior causes; avoid isolating a generation as if inorganic; present history as part of a living whole influenced by past and future events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish contemporary from later sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully to distinguish the contemporary sources of information for each period from the sources of later times, and to supply...comment as will enable the student to form a fairly accurate notion of each author's value as an authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In historical studies supply bibliographic/critical accounts that separate primary (contemporary) sources from later accounts and assess authorial value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey/report structure: divide regionally and publish district monographs
rubrics_metrics.description: The present report reviews the operations of the survey during 1879-'80 in the four geological districts into which Mr. King has divided his work...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divide large survey work into clear districts, describe them in text, and define them on a map; include monographs on particular features in each district authored by the responsible assistant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine survey data with economic/resource information
rubrics_metrics.description: Information of a general character respecting mining resources and industries has been derived from officers of the Census Bureau, whose co-operation Mr. King enjoyed, and is added to the special reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For practical survey reports, include relevant economic/resource information and note inter-agency cooperation where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fill gaps in language-specific literature
rubrics_metrics.description: This book supplies a want, there being no work in English that treats of sugar analysis ... it is not always convenient for the chemist to have to depend upon German and French treatises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A useful manual should bring material up to date in the target language and offer fuller treatment where existing sources are scattered or inaccessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive monograph: include literature review and practical guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The author ... has apparently embodied in this volume all the lore on the subject, giving the color of justice to the publisher's assertion that it is the most complete and exhaustive monograph ever published upon any game-fish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine extensive review of prior literature, original descriptions, and practical sections (e.g., methods, tools, tackle) to produce an authoritative monograph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical art manuals: point out common errors and economical practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A manual of suggestions, adapted to practical application ... seeks to point out errors in the present systems of drawing the figure — errors arising out of unconsidered conditions of placement and pose; to explain what is natural and what is merely conventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For art manuals, emphasize practical application, error identification, and time‑economizing methods for students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soil analysis principle: productivity proportional to available plant-food
rubrics_metrics.description: Other things being equal, productiveness is, or should be, sensibly proportional to the amount of available plant-food within reach of the roots during the period of the plant's development, provided that such supply does not exceed the maximum of that which the plant can utilize, when the surplus simply remains inert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret soil analyses in terms of the quantity of plant-available nutrients within root reach during growth, not merely total constituent amounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse accessible/assimilable amounts not total contents
rubrics_metrics.description: For finding the exact value of the soil from analysis, it is necessary, however, not so much to find the actual amounts of the constituents in the soil, as to find the amounts which are accessible to and assimilable by the plants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use extraction/solvent methods that reflect plant availability rather than total chemical composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select solvents to represent plant action
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem is, then, to find a solvent which shall as nearly as possible represent the action of the plant itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose analytical solvents that mimic root/plant uptake to estimate available nutrients accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for absence of virgin soils when generalizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses of European soils fail because virgin soils do not exist in Europe, and no generalizations can be drawn from the examination of any spot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious drawing generalizations from soils that have long been cultivated/altered; prefer regions with undisturbed native vegetation where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use native vegetation as an observational starting point
rubrics_metrics.description: Professor Hilgard's method of analysis starts from the observation of the productive qualities of the soil as indicated by the native growth. He then tries to ascertain what are the peculiarities of the soil that favor this kind of growth...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin soil evaluation by observing native plant growth, then investigate soil properties that favor that growth compared with others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include mechanical/physical soil conditions in evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: A loose soil, by enlarging the sphere of expansion of the roots may enable them to reach as large quantities of food, even when it is more widely scattered, as they can find in a more highly charged but more compact and less penetrable soil. Hence mechanical conditions should always be taken into account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess texture, compaction and penetrability of soils alongside chemical measures, since physical properties affect root access to nutrients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize lime as a primary fertility factor
rubrics_metrics.description: The thriftiness or present productiveness of a soil is measurably dependent on the presence of a certain minimum quantity of lime. The evidence on this point is 'overwhelming.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate soils for a threshold level of lime; consider lime's multiple chemical and physical effects when assessing fertility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand mechanisms of lime's beneficial effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The lime operates by effecting the more rapid transformation of vegetable matter into active humus, by retaining the humus against the oxidizing influence of hot climates; by rendering minute percentages of phosphoric acid and potash effective; by a tendency to secure the proper maintenance of the conditions of nitrification; and, physically, by promoting the flocculation of the soil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When recommending lime, explain its roles in humus formation, nutrient availability, nitrification conditions, and soil physical structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rank nutrient importance: phosphoric acid after lime
rubrics_metrics.description: After that of lime, the proportion of phosphoric acid seems to be the most important factor in the productiveness of soils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize phosphoric acid evaluation and management once lime adequacy is addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potash: typically present; not first resort in exhausted soils
rubrics_metrics.description: A certain percentage of potash is required, but it is present in most soils; and Professor Hilgard infers, generally, that 'potash manures are not among the first to be sought for after the soils have become 'tired' by exhaustive culture.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not default to potash manures first in restoring exhausted soils; assess actual potash status before application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate iron's form and distribution, not just percent
rubrics_metrics.description: Iron, in the shape of ferric hydrate finely diffused, appears to be an important ingredient... The efficiency of the hydrate depends essentially upon a state of fine division; and when merely incrusting the sand-grains, or aggregated into bog-ore grains, it exerts little or no influence, although the analysis may show a high percentage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess ferruginous soils for fine division / physical state of iron; recognize limits when iron occurs as coarse aggregates or incrustations and consider drainage vulnerabilities of ferruginous soils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stratigraphic correlation: compare exposures and relate to typics
rubrics_metrics.description: For this purpose he has given comparative reviews of the examinations of various exposures... The author intends to discuss in a future paper the relations of these deposits to those of other parts of the United States, and to correlate them, if possible, with the typical Eocene deposits of Europe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine depth and relative position by comparative review of multiple exposures and seek correlations with well-described type-sections elsewhere to fix stratigraphic placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stratigraphic description should record lithology, fossils, and thickness
rubrics_metrics.description: The Alabama Eocene deposits are arranged ... 4. 'White Limestone' ... not very abundant in fossils, 50 or more feet; 3. The fossiliferous arenaceous deposit ... very rich in fossils, 17 feet; 2. Buhrstone ... about 250 or more feet; 1. The Wood's Bluff and Bashia deposits ... consisting of alternating dark clays, greenish and buff sands, and numerous seams of lignite ... 50 or more feet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting stratigraphic schemes, list lithologic units, fossil content, depositional character (subaqueous/terrestrial), and measured or estimated thicknesses for each unit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field identification: account for seasonal and habitat color variation
rubrics_metrics.description: The color of snakes depends upon the season when they change their skins... The color also varies much with the habitat. Thus, the death-adder is nearly red in a red-soil country, black and gray in black soil, and brown on sand...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In field descriptions and identifications, note that animal coloration can vary seasonally and geographically with habitat; do not rely on color alone for species identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Camouflage affects detectability; use indirect signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing is more remarkable about snakes than their extraordinary faculty of making themselves invisible... Their presence was known by the casts of their skins which they left, for two years, without being seen or heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveyors should use indirect evidence (e.g., casts, tracks) and be aware that cryptic animals may be easily overlooked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epidemiological analysis: identify origin and contributing social factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hawaiian leprosy was introduced from China with the coolie-trade, and was first recognized in 1848. Its spread has been furthered by the peculiar habits of the people, particularly in eating, and their close association in their houses, and is contributed to by the exhaustion caused by the use of the intoxicant kava. To this may be added impure vaccination... and the prevalent licentiousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing disease spread, trace introduction pathways and enumerate social, hygienic, and medical practices that could contribute; include consideration of cultural behaviors and medical practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disease classification and transmission claims should be stated clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: All observers agree that the disease is hereditary and that death alone ends it. It is established that it is a specific and well-marked disease — not a form of syphilis — that it exists in two varieties, the tubercular and anaesthetic, which may be distinct or associated, that it is not contagious, but is transplantable, and that men are more liable to it than women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State consensus views on heredity, types/varieties, contagion/transplantability, and sex susceptibility when summarizing or reporting on a disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevention and treatment recommendations should be evidence-linked
rubrics_metrics.description: The most useful drug in affording relief being the bark of the hoang-nan-tree. The most effective preventive of the spread of the disease is isolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When recommending therapeutics or public health measures, cite observed efficacy and practical feasibility (e.g., isolation) and discuss likely outcomes (e.g., potential to stamp out disease if isolation maintained).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public health risk assessment must consider travel/trade and social practices
rubrics_metrics.description: The population of the Pacific States are in no immediate danger from leprosy, but the increasing intercourse with China and the Sandwich Islands, combined with prostitution, offers a constant menace, and makes vigilance a duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess regional risk by considering patterns of travel, trade, migration, and social practices; make recommendations for surveillance and vigilance accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority claims require documented earlier publications and reproductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Dr. Alter's papers on spectrum analysis were published in the 'American Journal of Science' in 1854 and 1855, five years before Kirchhoff announced his discoveries. An abstract of the first paper was published in Liebig and Kopp's 'Chemico-Jahresberichte' for 1854. The second was reproduced in 'L'Institut' in 1856 and in other journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish scientific priority by documenting dates and venues of original publication and by locating reprints/abstracts in other contemporaneous journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skeptical standards for extraordinary microscopic claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Professor Smith expresses a strong disbelief in the alleged discovery by Professor Hahn of organic remains in meteoric stones... the well-known chemical composition of these bodies is averse to the existence of any such remains... Were these remains present, we should discover carbonate of lime in their interior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require chemical consistency (e.g., carbonate of lime) and rule out surface incrustations when evaluating claims of organics in meteorites; beware of misleading resemblances from igneous mineral textures and of observers 'imagination' running wild.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscopic interpretation: differentiate mineral textures from organics
rubrics_metrics.description: In the microscopic examination the two predominating minerals, enstatite and bronzite, will, by their fissures and forms, sometimes remind one of vegetable and other organic forms, but the merest tyro of an observer will trace here nothing but a rare resemblance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train observers to recognize igneous mineral structures that can mimic organic forms and insist on corroborating chemical/mineralogical evidence before accepting organic identifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental design: include multiple treatment groups and controls
rubrics_metrics.description: A conservatory was built ... plants were disposed in four groups, each receiving a different treatment: (1) deprived of the light of day and exposed to electric light all the time; (2) diffused daylight by day and electric light at night; (3) only diluted daylight by day and left in the dark at night; (4) kept during the day in a shaded garden-bed and taken into the conservatory and exposed to ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To test effects of a treatment (electric light) on plants, use multiple groups to isolate the variable against different light regimes and include appropriate day/night comparisons and shaded controls.
